prompt: A complete binary tree (every level full except possibly the last, which fills from the left) holds 1,000 nodes and has height 9. You keep adding nodes in the same complete shape until it holds 2,000. What happens to its height?

options.explanation: Height would double only if each level held a fixed number of nodes. Here each level can hold twice as many as the one above, so doubling the nodes adds a level rather than doubling the height.
Height 9 holds at most 1,023 nodes (levels of 1, 2, 4 … 512). Once the tree passes that, a new level must start.

options.text: It grows by exactly one level, to 10
options.explanation: Correct. Each new level can hold as many nodes as all the levels above it put together, plus one. Height 10 holds up to 2,047 nodes, so 2,000 nodes fit with just one extra level.

options.text: It grows by about 1,000, because each new node adds depth
options.explanation: That describes a chain where every node has one child. A complete tree fills each level across before starting the next one.

workedExample:
1. In a binary tree, each level can hold at most twice as many nodes as the level above: 1, 2, 4, 8, … 512 for levels 0 to 9.
2. Those ten levels add up to 1,023, so a complete tree of 1,000 nodes has height 9: its last level is nearly full.
3. The next level, level 10, can hold another 1,024 nodes on its own. Adding 1,000 more nodes fills most of that one level, and the total of 2,000 is below the 2,047 that height 10 allows.
4. So the height goes from 9 to 10. Doubling the node count adds one level, which is what logarithmic height means in practice: about 20 levels for a million nodes, 30 for a billion.

prompt: Two binary trees each hold 1,000 nodes. Tree X has height 9 and tree Y has height 999 (heights in edges). Which statement is right?

options.text: Y cannot hold only 1,000 nodes: a height of 999 needs more nodes than that
options.explanation: A tall tree does not need many nodes. A chain where every node has one child gains a level per node, so 1,000 nodes in a chain have height 999.

options.text: X must be a perfect tree, with every level completely full
options.explanation: A perfect tree of height 9 has exactly 1,023 nodes. X has 1,000, so its last level is not full; it can still be as short as possible, for example as a complete tree.

options.text: X is as short as any 1,000-node binary tree can be, and Y is a chain with one node per level
options.explanation: Correct. Height 8 can hold at most 511 nodes, so 9 is the minimum for 1,000 nodes. Height 999 is the maximum: every node has at most one child, so the tree is a chain.

options.text: Their heights differ, but a search that follows one root-to-leaf path takes about the same time in both
options.explanation: A path-following search costs time proportional to the height, so Y can take about 1,000 steps where X takes about 10. That gap is the whole reason balancing exists.

workedExample:
1. Shortest possible: levels hold at most 1, 2, 4 … nodes, so height 8 fits at most 511 nodes and height 9 fits up to 1,023. 1,000 nodes need height at least 9, and X achieves it.
2. Tallest possible: a tree is tallest when it is a chain, one node per level. 1,000 nodes then span 999 edges, so Y must be a chain (each node has at most one child).
3. X need not be perfect: a perfect height-9 tree would hold 1,023 nodes, not 1,000.
4. Consequence: an operation that walks one root-to-leaf path visits at most 10 nodes in X but up to 1,000 in Y.
